name: Najdi Ardah

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A cultural historian or traditional practitioner.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Sword and the Verse: Saudi Arabia's Najdi Ardah
This is Najdi Ardah. Pre-battle origin.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (LbbNhRabztI)
Title card: Najdi Ardah · Saudi Arabia · Pre-battle origin

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in the Najd region as a pre-battle ritual to display tribal fighting strength and boost morale.
It has since transitioned into a celebratory practice for national and personal milestones.
on_screen: Map: Saudi Arabia · Middle East
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It marks the beginning or end of important occasions, serving as a symbol of group cohesion and cultural heritage.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Men stand in two rows facing each other.
They perform rhythmic body sways from front to back and lift swords from top to bottom.
The movement is synchronized with chanted poetry and drum beats.
Watch for Sword lift.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (LbbNhRabztI)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Two rows of men facing each other with an open space in the center.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music consists of chanted poetry and percussion.
Large drums are played first, followed by smaller drums, creating a layered rhythmic structure.
Listen for the large drums, small drums.
A combination of deep, resonant drum beats followed by higher-pitched percussion, overlaid with the rhythmic chanting of poetry.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Participants wear traditional Saudi attire and carry light swords.
A flag-bearer is present in the center, and the performance takes place at weddings, births, graduations, and national events.

Part of the broader Arabian Peninsula 'ardah' tradition.

music_brief.sound_description: A combination of deep, resonant drum beats followed by higher-pitched percussion, overlaid with the rhythmic chanting of poetry.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Najdi Ardah (Saudi Arabia). Instruments: large drums, small drums. Vocal style: Chanted poetry with a refrain repeated by the group.. Form: Call and response between a lead poet and the group.. Mood: celebratory, rhythmic, communal. It should sound like this: A combination of deep, resonant drum beats followed by higher-pitched percussion, overlaid with the rhythmic chanting of poetry. rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
